predictions.rationale:
Arkansas is the better pick based on the matchup of top-end talent, offensive pressure, and defensive tools described in the reports. The clearest separator is Darius Acuff Jr. Hawai‘i’s report explicitly raises concern about facing opponents with the best late-game guard on the floor, and Arkansas has exactly that in an elite primary creator who averages 22.9 points and 6.4 assists, shoots 44.5% from three, and has already shown he can carry high-end games with 49 at Alabama, 31 against Auburn, and 28 points with 13 assists versus Texas. In a tournament setting, the team with the most reliable half-court shot creator often has the edge, and Arkansas has the most dynamic individual scorer and playmaker in this game by a wide margin.

Arkansas also appears better equipped to stress Hawai‘i’s defensive structure than most Big West opponents. Hawai‘i is described as a contain-and-finish-possession defense that does not gamble much, protects the arc well, and rebounds effectively. That profile is strong, but Arkansas’ offense is built specifically around dribble-drive pressure, paint touches, and free-throw generation. The Razorbacks attempted 794 free throws in 34 games, scored 52 paint points against Auburn, and produced 38 fastbreak points against Texas. Acuff’s downhill game, plus Richmond’s cutting and slashing, plus Ewin and Brazile as dive and pop partners, gives Arkansas multiple ways to crack a defense that prefers to stay sound rather than disrupt. Hawai‘i’s defense may limit easy threes, but Arkansas does not need to live on jumpers; its preferred mode is collapsing the defense, getting to the rim, and living at the line.

The supporting-cast matchup also favors Arkansas. Hawai‘i is balanced and experienced, with six players between 8.5 and 14.1 points, but Arkansas has more individually dangerous pieces around its star. Meleek Thomas gives a second perimeter scorer at 15.4 points and 42.1% from three, Brazile is a two-way frontcourt problem with range and shot blocking, Richmond has emerged as a downhill finisher who just posted major scoring games late in the year, and Ewin is an efficient interior finisher and rim protector in limited minutes. That means Hawai‘i cannot simply load up on Acuff without risking clean finishes by Richmond, pick-and-pop or lob pressure from Brazile, and efficient interior scoring from Ewin.

Defensively, Arkansas also has matchup advantages against Hawai‘i’s offensive style. Hawai‘i’s offense is balanced and veteran-led, but the report notes one major concern: shot creation against length. Arkansas has exactly the sort of length and back-line rim protection that can make Hawai‘i uncomfortable. The Razorbacks allow only 31.7% from three, average 5.1 blocks, and can erase mistakes at the rim with Brazile and Ewin. Hawai‘i’s offense relies on multiple handlers, inside-out play, and late-clock veteran execution, but against Arkansas those late-clock possessions are more likely to end with contested pull-ups or drives into size. Hawai‘i has shown vulnerability when facing elite length and rim protection, most clearly in the overtime loss at UC Irvine when interior resistance blunted them late. Arkansas is not identical stylistically, but its combination of perimeter pressure, shot blocking, and transition offense points toward a similar kind of stress.

The biggest argument for Hawai‘i is that it rebounds well, defends the three, gets to the foul line, and has repeatedly won close games. Arkansas’ main documented weakness is against physical frontcourts that dominate the glass, as Florida did when it won the rebounding battle 51-31 and scored 56 paint points. If Hawai‘i could reproduce that kind of interior control, the upset path would be real. But the Hawai‘i report does not suggest a front line with overwhelming size or depth on the level of the SEC opponents that have physically punished Arkansas. Isaac Johnson is a quality interior anchor, and Hawai‘i has a strong rebound margin, but its offense is less overpowering than the teams that have given Arkansas the most trouble. Hawai‘i also was out-rebounded 38-27 by Long Beach State in one of its key late-season losses, which makes it harder to project a dominant glass advantage here.

Pace and athletic ceiling also tilt toward Arkansas. The Razorbacks have shown they can win in multiple environments: grinding out Tennessee with free throws, blasting Texas in transition, and flipping the script against Auburn with paint dominance and ball security. Hawai‘i has admirable versatility too, but the team’s losses suggest problems when opponents have downhill scoring and superior individual shot creation. Cal Poly jumped on UH early with dribble pressure, and Long Beach State exposed it with guard shot-making late. Arkansas is better than both in terms of raw talent and has more rim pressure than the typical Hawai‘i opponent.

Finally, the tournament-context factor favors Arkansas. Both teams are well coached, but the report highlights John Calipari’s extensive NCAA Tournament history, multiple Final Fours, and a roster structure that specifically resembles a typical dangerous March team: star lead guard, NBA-level wings, rim protection, and late-game creation. Hawai‘i is tough, experienced, and capable of hanging around, especially if it keeps the game in the half court and wins the foul-line and rebounding battle. But based only on these reports, Arkansas has more ways to win and the best singular matchup weapon in Acuff. The most likely outcome is that Hawai‘i competes for stretches with its discipline and veteran composure, but Arkansas’ shot creation, paint pressure, and defensive length eventually create separation.

Arkansas is the more likely winner because the matchup pits Hawaii’s biggest strength — disciplined halfcourt defense that suppresses eFG% and free throws — against an Arkansas offense that is unusually well-built to survive and even stress that style. The Razorbacks are not a one-dimensional high-major favorite; they average 89.9 points per game, shoot .500 from the field and .389 from three, commit only 9.0 turnovers per game, and post a 1.9 assist-turnover ratio. That combination matters against Hawaii specifically. Hawaii’s profile says it does not create many turnovers and instead wins by forcing misses, finishing possessions, and keeping teams off the line. But Arkansas has multiple counters: Darius Acuff Jr. is an elite primary creator and closer at 22.9 points and 6.4 assists per game with 44.5% three-point shooting, Meleek Thomas adds another perimeter scorer at 15.4 points and 42.1% from three, and Arkansas has two different screen partners in Trevon Brazile and Malique Ewin plus a downhill finisher in Billy Richmond III. That gives Arkansas more shot-creation diversity than the kind of opponent Hawaii usually sees.

The single most important matchup factor is Arkansas’s paint pressure versus Hawaii’s foul-avoidant defense. Hawaii’s defensive identity is built around allowing only a .227 opponent free-throw rate and making teams score over a set defense. But Arkansas’s offense is specifically described as a Calipari dribble-drive attack that got to the line 794 times in 34 games, an enormous volume. The Tennessee game is a strong example: Arkansas won by generating 25-of-27 free throws even without great second-half shooting. The Auburn rematch is another: 52 points in the paint, 27-of-40 on twos, and 19 assists against five turnovers. If Hawaii cannot keep Arkansas out of the lane, the Rainbow Warriors’ best statistical edge gets neutralized. Even if Hawaii succeeds somewhat in reducing free throws, Arkansas has enough efficient halfcourt scoring from Acuff, Thomas, Brazile, Richmond, and Ewin to score without living solely at the stripe.

Arkansas also appears better equipped to attack Hawaii’s defense than Hawaii is to solve Arkansas’s defense. Hawaii’s offense is only ordinary by the numbers: 110.0 ORtg, ranking around 170th nationally, with a balanced but not high-volume three-point profile and no indication of elite shot-making or explosive comeback ability. The report explicitly frames Hawaii as workmanlike rather than explosive. That is a problem against an Arkansas defense that holds opponents to .317 from three, averages 5.1 blocks and 7.3 steals, and is anchored by frontcourt rim protection from Brazile and Ewin. Arkansas does not need to gamble wildly to create defensive success; it can stay big, long, and disruptive around the rim. Since Hawaii’s likely path is to drag the game into a halfcourt possession war, it still needs enough offense to finish those possessions efficiently against length. Based on these reports alone, that is the shakier side of the matchup.

Another major separator is top-end shot creation. In tournament settings, when scouting is tight and possessions get late, the team with the best guard often wins. Arkansas clearly has that player in Acuff. He is not just productive; he has documented elite late-game shot-making and a proven ability to function in high-possession and clutch environments, including 49 points at Alabama, 31 against Auburn, and 28 points with 13 assists against Texas. Hawaii’s analysis, by contrast, is almost entirely team- and profile-based, with no comparable evidence of an individual creator who can consistently win late-clock possessions against SEC-level athleticism. That matters a great deal against Arkansas because even if Hawaii succeeds in slowing pace and making possessions ugly, Acuff gives Arkansas a bailout option that Hawaii’s report does not suggest it can match.

Hawaii is not without a real upset path. Their top-15-level defensive rating by Sports-Reference, strong opponent eFG suppression, decent defensive rebounding, and disciplined foul avoidance make them a legitimate style problem. If they can keep Arkansas out of transition, force the Razorbacks into a purely halfcourt game, and prevent the parade to the free-throw line, the game could stay close. Arkansas also has one identified weakness: physical frontcourts and rebounding pressure, as shown in the Florida loss where it was beaten badly on the glass and in paint points. But Hawaii’s report does not describe an overwhelming interior offense or dominant front line that is likely to reproduce that exact blueprint. Their offensive strength is not power scoring inside or elite spacing from deep; it is mainly adequacy supported by defense.

So the most likely game script is that Hawaii’s defense keeps the margin respectable for stretches, but Arkansas’s superior talent, better guard play, stronger transition ceiling, and more varied scoring options eventually win out. Arkansas has shown it can win in multiple ways — through free throws against Tennessee, paint dominance and ball security against Auburn, and transition bursts against Texas. Hawaii’s profile suggests a narrower path to victory built on turning the game into a lower-efficiency grind. Because Arkansas is both efficient enough in the halfcourt and explosive enough in transition to break that script, the Razorbacks are the better pick.

Arkansas is the better pick because the exact strengths in its profile line up with the specific pressure points in Hawai‘i’s profile. Arkansas plays fast, attacks the rim relentlessly, and is driven by an elite lead guard in Darius Acuff Jr., while Hawai‘i is most vulnerable when opponents force speed, spread the floor, and make its big lineups defend repeated ball screens in space. The Hawai‘i report explicitly says the blueprint against them is to use early drag screens, run after makes, and turn the game into a speed-and-space test; that is essentially Arkansas at its best. Arkansas already has named examples of thriving in those conditions, most notably the March 4 win over Texas with a 19-4 start, 38 fastbreak points, and 21 assists, and the Auburn rematch where the Razorbacks generated 52 paint points and dominated two-point efficiency.

Arkansas is the better pick based on the overall strength, schedule-tested profile, and the specific way its strengths line up against Hawaii’s vulnerabilities. The Razorbacks rate as a clear top-20 team across major predictive systems, with Arkansas listed around NET 15-18, KenPom 17, BPI 21, Torvik 20, and ELO 9, while also carrying an elite résumé built on a 26-8 record, 13-5 SEC mark, top-10 strength of schedule indicators, and no bad losses (8-8 Q1, 8-0 Q2, undefeated in Q3/Q4). That matters here because Hawaii, while experienced and well-coached, is coming from a much lower competitive tier and has already shown some trouble when facing high-end physicality, length, and shot-making guards.

The most important matchup factor is Arkansas’ identity as a rugged, possession-winning team. The Hogs are not described as a perimeter-dependent offense; instead, they generate value through rim pressure, physical play, and especially offensive rebounding, with a 32.2% offensive rebound rate. Hawaii’s defense is built to contain, avoid gambling, and finish possessions with rebounds, and that is one of its biggest strengths. But the report also shows that when Hawaii loses control physically, problems surface: Long Beach State out-rebounded UH 38-27 in the March 7 loss, and UC Irvine’s length and rim protection blunted Hawaii late in the January 29 overtime defeat. Arkansas is exactly the type of opponent that can stress Hawaii in those same areas by attacking the paint and creating second chances.

Arkansas’ résumé also suggests a much higher baseline level of performance. Even if its possession-by-possession profile is a bit less dominant than public perception, it still projects as a balanced top-20-caliber team from a major conference that played a top-10 schedule and closed the year 8-2 with a five-game winning streak. Hawaii’s case is built more on veteran execution, close-game poise, and a sturdy Big West profile. Those are real assets, but they are less reliable against a team with Arkansas’ athleticism and depth of competition. Hawaii has repeatedly won tight games, but needing late-clock creation and clutch shot-making is dangerous against an SEC opponent that is battle-tested and likely superior in talent.

There are also reasons to think Arkansas can challenge Hawaii’s offensive structure. Hawaii depends on balanced scoring, veteran guards, free-throw pressure, and late-clock decision-making. But the report notes a concern about Hawaii’s shot creation against length and whether it can survive when the opponent has the best late-game guard on the floor. Arkansas’ overall athletic profile and high-level competition suggest it is more likely to impose that kind of pressure than a Big West opponent. Hawaii’s offense has also shown cold-start vulnerability, as in the UCSB loss when it missed 13 of its first 14 shots, and it struggled when stronger defensive length took away clean finishes and late-game rhythm.

Hawaii does have pathways to make this competitive. Its defense holds opponents to .411 shooting and .304 from three, it rebounds well on the defensive end, and it has multiple proven clutch performers in Erickson, Bullock, Johnson, and Rouhliadeff. If Hawaii can protect the defensive glass, force Arkansas into a jump-shooting game, and keep it within a possession late, the Rainbow Warriors have enough experience to threaten an upset. But based solely on these reports, Arkansas is more trustworthy because it combines strong predictive quality, a much tougher résumé, excellent recent form, and a physical style that directly attacks the kind of weaknesses Hawaii has shown in its most telling losses. Hawaii looks dangerous and disciplined, but Arkansas looks like the more complete and better-tested team.

Arkansas should be favored based solely on these reports because it owns the substantially stronger overall team profile, the far better schedule-tested résumé, and a style that directly pressures one of Hawaii’s key defensive dependencies. The clearest separator is tier of team quality: Arkansas is consistently rated as a top-20 caliber team by major predictive systems (NET 15-18, KenPom 17, BPI 21, Torvik 20, ELO 9), while Hawaii clusters around 95-110 nationally (NET 95, KenPom 103, BPI 100, Torvik 110, ELO 101). That gap is too large to ignore. Arkansas also played and won against dramatically tougher opposition, with schedule strength around top-10 to top-16 overall and top-6 to top-27 out of conference depending on metric, plus strong quadrant results including 8-8 in Q1 and no bad losses. Hawaii, by contrast, built its profile against a very weak schedule, with SOS around 232 by Sports-Reference, NET SOS 316, and non-conference SOS 357. That means Hawaii’s strong defensive numbers come with much less certainty when projected up against an SEC-level opponent.

The matchup specifics also lean Arkansas. Hawaii’s best trait is defense: a 96.5 defensive rating, elite opponent eFG% suppression (.438), low opponent free-throw rate (.227), and solid defensive rebounding control. But Arkansas is not a finesse, three-point-dependent offense that can be easily neutralized by merely running shooters off the line. The Razorbacks’ offensive identity is built more around physicality, rim pressure, and second chances. Their 32.2% offensive rebound rate is one of their defining strengths, and that is especially important against a Hawaii team that wins by forcing misses and ending possessions. If Arkansas can partially break that possession-ending formula with offensive rebounding, it attacks Hawaii exactly where an underdog most needs defensive completeness. Arkansas does not need to shoot an overwhelming volume of threes to score; in fact, its relatively modest 35.2% three-point attempt rate suggests it is comfortable playing through the paint and the glass. That gives it a more stable path to offense than a jump-shot-heavy favorite would have.

Arkansas also appears more balanced overall. Even though its public profile is described as strong rather than elite, the Razorbacks still look like an above-average team on both ends, with a 52.2% eFG%, strong offensive rebounding, top-20 predictive support, and a +14.3 advanced net rating. Hawaii is more one-dimensional by comparison: the defense is excellent, but the offense is only ordinary, with a 110.0 offensive rating ranked 170th nationally. That matters a lot in an upset attempt. If Hawaii’s defense slips even modestly against Arkansas’ size, athleticism, and offensive rebounding, there is less evidence that Hawaii has the offensive ceiling to compensate. Their offensive profile is functional rather than explosive: .528 eFG%, 16.0 turnover rate, 31.5 offensive rebound rate, .321 free-throw rate, and a .321 three-point attempt rate that indicates they are not especially built to erase deficits with volume perimeter variance. Against a stronger, battle-tested opponent, that limited offensive gear set is a major concern.

Recent form strengthens the Arkansas case further. The Razorbacks entered the tournament 26-8, had gone 8-2 in their last 10, and were on a five-game winning streak. That suggests they were rounding into form late. Hawaii also had momentum through its Big West tournament title, but the report explicitly frames them as solid rather than dominant down the stretch, and again, that form came against a much softer caliber of competition.

There is still an upset path for Hawaii. Its defense is good enough to drag Arkansas into an ugly game, especially if it protects the defensive glass better than usual, keeps Arkansas out of the paint, and forces the Razorbacks into lower-efficiency jump shooting. The report specifically notes Arkansas can become more vulnerable if second-chance points and interior pressure are neutralized. But based on the totality of the evidence, Arkansas has more ways to win: superior baseline quality, far stronger résumé indicators, better recent form, more physical shot creation, and a strong offensive rebounding edge that threatens Hawaii’s preferred game script. Hawaii looks like a live underdog stylistically, but Arkansas is the more likely winner.

Arkansas is the better pick based on the combination of overall team quality and how its strengths line up with Hawai‘i’s vulnerabilities. The Arkansas report describes a clear top-20 team by the main predictive systems, with résumé markers even stronger than that: NET 15-18 range, ELO No. 9, RPI No. 7, overall SOS No. 9, non-conference SOS No. 6, and excellent quadrant results highlighted by 8-8 in Q1 and zero losses outside Q1. That profile suggests a battle-tested SEC team that consistently handled the level of opponent Hawai‘i more closely resembles, while also proving it can compete with high-end teams. Arkansas also enters on strong form, having gone 8-2 in its last 10 with a five-game winning streak, which matters against a Hawai‘i team stepping up from the Big West into a much more physical and athletic matchup.

The biggest matchup edge is that Arkansas appears built to attack exactly where Hawai‘i is most stress-prone. Arkansas is described as pressure-and-glass oriented, with a strong 32.2% offensive rebounding rate and a style based on rim pressure, physicality, and second chances rather than relying on pure three-point shooting. Hawai‘i is also big and physical, but the scouting report says the best way to beat the Rainbow Warriors is to speed them up, pressure the ball, and force them to handle repeated screening and transition situations. Arkansas’ style strongly suggests it can do that. Hawai‘i’s turnover profile is shaky enough to matter against a team with SEC-level athletic pressure: 13.5 turnovers per game and a 16.80% turnover rate, without a truly steady low-turnover lead guard. The report specifically notes that Hawai‘i can be disrupted by pressure and cites collapses such as the 17-0 UC San Diego run after halftime. Arkansas, as a rugged possession-winning team, is well positioned to create those kinds of live-ball mistakes and momentum swings.

Arkansas also has the offensive identity to challenge Hawai‘i’s defensive structure. Hawai‘i wants games played in controlled half-court segments where its size can protect the paint and dominate physically. But the Hawai‘i report is explicit that opponents should use early drag screens, run after makes, and make Johnson and the larger forwards sprint through repeated ball-screen coverages. Arkansas may not be a spacing-heavy three-point attack, but it does create value through interior pressure and offensive rebounding, which can stress Hawai‘i’s frontcourt mobility and floor balance. Even if Arkansas is not an elite shooting team, its 52.2% effective field goal percentage and offensive rebounding strength mean it can still score efficiently through the exact areas where Hawai‘i can be made uncomfortable: repeated paint attacks, physical possessions, and second shots.

Defensively, Arkansas should have a favorable script. Hawai‘i’s offense is balanced and size-based, but the team shoots only 31.5% from three, with key perimeter scorers like Bullock and Kerr well below strong efficiency from deep. The Hawai‘i analysis says the correct plan is to crowd the lane, go under against inconsistent shooters, deny Johnson clean post catches, and force a jump-shooting game from the guards. Arkansas appears capable of doing exactly that. Since Arkansas is not dependent on high-volume threes itself and instead wins with physicality and possession control, it should be comfortable in a bruising game while still being able to shrink the paint against Hawai‘i’s offense. Hawai‘i’s strengths on the interior are real, but the report makes clear that if Johnson is tagged and the guards are pushed into making shots over the top, the offense can bog down.

There is some risk because Arkansas is not described as a dominant top-five efficiency machine, and Hawai‘i’s size and defense could make scoring choppy. If Hawai‘i successfully turns the game into a low-possession wrestling match and controls the defensive glass, Arkansas’ modest three-point volume could cap its offensive ceiling. But overall, the balance still favors Arkansas because it owns the superior résumé, has been tested against much stronger competition, enters hotter, and matches up well with Hawai‘i’s most visible weaknesses: ball-pressure vulnerability, suspect guard shooting, and discomfort when opponents increase pace and force big lineups to defend in space. Based solely on these reports, Arkansas is the more likely winner.

Arkansas is the more likely winner because its primary strengths line up directly against the areas where Hawai‘i is most vulnerable. The Razorbacks have an elite, organized transition-and-drive offense built around Darius Acuff Jr. (22.9 ppg, 6.5 apg, .486/.445/.804), and they combine that star creation with excellent efficiency (.500 FG, .389 from three), strong ball security (only 9.0 turnovers per game), and major fast-break production (19.25 fast-break points per game, listed third nationally in Arkansas’ notes). That is a difficult profile for Hawai‘i because UH’s defense is described as a contain-and-finish-possession unit rather than a high-disruption one: Hawai‘i averages only 6.6 steals, does not rely on gambling, and is at its best when it can force a half-court game, wall off the lane, and clean the glass. Arkansas’ low-turnover, pace-with-organization style is specifically built to avoid giving that kind of defense easy control over tempo.

The biggest matchup edge is at lead guard. Hawai‘i has veteran creators and clutch players, but the report repeatedly notes concern about defending elite shot-making guards late, with the Long Beach State loss serving as a clear warning: once the first wave of pressure stopped producing turnovers, UH became vulnerable to a hot perimeter creator. Arkansas brings exactly that problem in Acuff, whose offense is not just scoring but paint collapse and kick-out creation. Since Arkansas also has secondary shooting from Meleek Thomas (.421 from three) and additional spacing from players like Karter Knox, Hawai‘i cannot simply overcommit to Acuff without risking clean perimeter looks. Arkansas’ offense is also not overly dependent on isolation from the start; with 578 assists on 1091 made field goals, it functions as team offense until late-clock moments, where Acuff can then take over individually. That combination is especially dangerous in a tournament setting.

Hawai‘i does have traits that could make the game competitive. Its defensive rebounding, three-point defense (.304 opponent 3PT), and overall physicality are the exact kinds of attributes that have bothered Arkansas at times. The Arkansas report is explicit that the best way to beat the Razorbacks is to win the glass decisively, force them into a one-shot half-court game, and make Acuff finish over length instead of spraying passes. Hawai‘i’s +6.4 rebound margin, top-35 caliber defensive rebounding, 39.3 rebounds per game, and veteran frontcourt led by Isaac Johnson and Harry Rouhliadeff suggest it is more capable than many mid-majors of executing part of that formula. Hawai‘i also gets to the line frequently, which can help slow pace and keep Arkansas out of rhythm.

But the problem for Hawai‘i is that the Arkansas losses cited in the report generally came against teams with overwhelming high-major physicality on the glass and at the rim—Florida winning the rebounding battle 51-31, Auburn 37-28, and Kentucky 35-26. Hawai‘i is solid and disciplined, but nothing in the analysis suggests it has the same level of frontcourt force that those SEC opponents used to overwhelm Arkansas physically. The UH report itself notes issues when facing elite length and rim protection, as in the UC Irvine overtime loss, and concerns about whether Hawai‘i can generate enough shot creation when the opponent has the best late-game guard on the floor. Against Arkansas, that concern is magnified because Acuff is clearly the best perimeter shot-maker and creator in the matchup.

Another decisive factor is pace control. Hawai‘i’s best path is to turn the game into a grind, but Arkansas has evidence that pressing them is not an effective primary lever because they protect the ball so well and are 13-1 when they keep turnovers in single digits. If Hawai‘i cannot manufacture live-ball turnovers, Arkansas is likely to get into its preferred early offense often enough to create separation. And while Hawai‘i defends the three well in aggregate, Arkansas has the kind of shooting personnel to punish a defense that collapses too far into the lane. Conversely, Hawai‘i’s offense is balanced and experienced, but it is not described as having a single unstoppable creator who can consistently bend Arkansas’ defense possession after possession. If the game becomes one where both teams need to score efficiently rather than merely execute late, Arkansas has the much higher offensive ceiling.

So while Hawai‘i’s maturity, rebounding, free-throw pressure, and clutch experience give it a credible upset pathway, Arkansas is the better pick because it has the most dominant individual weapon, the more explosive and efficient offense, superior transition production, and enough shooting and structure to prevent Hawai‘i from fully dictating a slow, low-possession game. Hawai‘i can stay within range if it wins the glass and keeps Arkansas in the half court, but based on these reports, Arkansas is more likely to impose its style than Hawai‘i is to impose its own.

Arkansas is the stronger pick based on the combination of superior top-end talent, offensive efficiency, and matchup-specific evidence from the reports. The Razorbacks have an elite tournament-caliber offensive engine in Darius Acuff Jr., who averages 22.9 points and 6.5 assists on .486/.445/.804 shooting, and they surround him with real secondary weapons in Meleek Thomas (.421 from three), Trevon Brazile (13.2 points, 7.4 rebounds, 53 blocks), and Malique Ewin (.591 FG). Team-wide, Arkansas scores 89.9 points per game, shoots .500 from the field and .389 from three, posts 17.0 assists against only 9.0 turnovers, and generates 19.25 fast-break points per game. That profile suggests a high-level offense that is both explosive and organized, not sloppy or overly dependent on chaos.

Hawaii does have a credible path to making this uncomfortable. Its defensive profile is the best argument for the underdog: a 96.5 defensive rating, only a .438 opponent eFG%, a 27.3 opponent offensive rebounding rate, and a .227 opponent free-throw rate. The report correctly identifies Hawaii as a style problem because it can force opponents into a halfcourt game, make them score over disciplined defense, and avoid gifting points at the line. That matters especially because Arkansas is at its most vulnerable when opponents shrink the floor, wall off the lane, and force it to operate against a set defense for long stretches. Arkansas also has shown some vulnerability when opponents win the glass decisively, as seen in losses to Auburn and Florida.

But based solely on these reports, Hawaii does not project as the ideal version of the anti-Arkansas blueprint. The Arkansas report says the best formula against the Razorbacks is to dominate the glass, attack their frontcourt physically with true size, and make every possession start against five defenders. Hawaii’s numbers show they are solid on the boards, but not overwhelmingly so: a 31.5 offensive rebounding rate on offense and 27.3 opponent offensive rebounding rate allowed on defense are good, yet nothing in the Hawaii analysis suggests the kind of elite, bruising rebounding edge that Florida (+20 on the glass) or Auburn (+9, plus major paint and second-chance advantages) imposed on Arkansas. Likewise, Hawaii’s offense is described as ordinary rather than explosive, with a 110.0 ORtg ranked 170th nationally, balanced but not bomb-heavy shot selection, and limited ability to erase deficits quickly.

That offensive limitation is crucial. Even if Hawaii’s defense succeeds in slowing Arkansas somewhat, Hawaii still has to score enough to capitalize. The report repeatedly characterizes Hawaii as a defense-first team with a soft schedule, consensus rankings around 100, and an offense that is more functional than dangerous. Against Arkansas, that means Hawaii would likely need to keep the game in a narrow scoring band throughout. That is difficult against a Razorback team that can punish soft zone, has multiple creators and finishers, and almost never beats itself with turnovers. Arkansas averages just 9.0 turnovers per game and is specifically noted as not broadly vulnerable to pressure; they are 13-1 when keeping turnovers to single digits. Since Hawaii’s defense is built more on shot suppression and discipline than on generating a high turnover rate, it is not naturally attacking one of Arkansas’s biggest strengths.

The talent gap at the top also favors Arkansas heavily. Hawaii’s best route is to make Acuff finish over length instead of creating for others, but Arkansas has enough perimeter shooting and interior finishing to stress even strong halfcourt defenses. Acuff’s shot-making, Thomas’s spacing, Brazile’s athleticism, and Ewin’s efficiency give Arkansas more ways to score than the kind of one-dimensional favorite that a defense-first mid-major can ambush. Arkansas also has evidence of adaptability under Calipari, including tournament wins on short turnarounds and successful adjustments in rematches, which strengthens confidence that they can respond if Hawaii initially drags the game into a grinder.

In short, Hawaii is live enough to reduce efficiency and make the game more competitive than a typical major-vs-mid-major matchup, but Arkansas still has the better overall case. Arkansas has the elite lead guard, the cleaner offensive profile, stronger supporting cast, much higher scoring ceiling, and no obvious turnover weakness for Hawaii to exploit. Unless Hawaii can produce a decisive rebounding and physicality edge beyond what its own report suggests, Arkansas’s offensive quality should eventually overwhelm Hawaii’s more limited scoring capacity.

Arkansas is the more likely winner because its core strengths line up directly against Hawai‘i’s clearest weaknesses. The Arkansas report describes an elite, guard-driven offense that scores 89.9 points per game, shoots .500 from the field and .389 from three, and takes exceptional care of the ball with only 9.0 turnovers per game and a 1.9 assist/turnover ratio. Darius Acuff Jr. is the central matchup problem: 22.9 points and 6.5 assists per game on .486/.445/.804 shooting. That profile is especially dangerous against a Hawai‘i team whose report identifies ball-pressure vulnerability, 13.5 turnovers per game, and difficulty when opponents speed the game up and force their big lineups into repeated transition and ball-screen coverage situations.

The biggest stylistic edge is pace and shot creation. Arkansas wants a fast, spaced, organized game and averages 19.25 fast-break points per game while allowing only 10.25. Hawai‘i, by contrast, is most comfortable in controlled half-court games where its size can matter on the glass and around the rim. The Hawai‘i analysis explicitly says the way to beat them is to run after makes and misses, use early drag screens, and force Johnson and the larger forwards to sprint into coverage. That is almost exactly Arkansas’ natural identity. Arkansas does not need to become something different to exploit Hawai‘i; its preferred style already attacks Hawai‘i’s discomfort points.

Acuff’s lead-guard advantage is likely decisive. Hawai‘i has size across the lineup, but the report says Erickson is solid rather than overwhelming athletically and that quick downhill guards can attack his feet and force help. Arkansas has precisely that kind of initiator in Acuff, plus secondary shotmaking from Meleek Thomas and finishing from Trevon Brazile and Malique Ewin. If Hawai‘i shrinks the floor to stop Acuff’s drives, Arkansas has the perimeter shooting to punish it: Acuff at .445 from three, Thomas at .421, Knox at .377, and the team at .389 overall. Hawai‘i’s own defensive recipe is built around paint protection and size, but Arkansas has enough spacing and creation to compromise that structure.

The turnover contrast also strongly favors Arkansas. The Arkansas analysis specifically says there is not strong evidence they are vulnerable to pressure; in fact, they routinely post single-digit turnover games and are 13-1 when doing so. Hawai‘i, on the other hand, is described as a team that can be bothered by pressure and whose offensive rhythm can collapse into opponent runs when ball security slips. In a tournament setting, that matters because Arkansas can both protect its own possessions and create the kind of tempo and stress that increases Hawai‘i’s mistakes. That combination makes it hard for Hawai‘i to control game shape.

Hawai‘i does have one real pathway: win physically on the glass, wall off the lane, and force Arkansas into a one-shot half-court game. The Arkansas report is clear that the best teams against them—Auburn, Florida, Kentucky—won the rebounding battle decisively and made Arkansas play against a set defense. Hawai‘i’s roster size, with Isaac Johnson at 7-0 and multiple 6-8 to 6-10 forwards, gives them a theoretical chance to test that vulnerability. Bullock’s 5.8 rebounds per game from the guard line and the team’s general length could help them generate second chances and slow Arkansas down.

But based solely on these reports, Hawai‘i’s strengths do not look overwhelming enough to consistently impose that script. Their offense is only a 31.5% three-point shooting team overall, with several guards identified as unreliable perimeter shooters. The Arkansas report says the way to beat Hawai‘i is to crowd the lane, go under, and force jump shooting from guards rather than post touches and paint catches. Arkansas has the athletic frontcourt pieces in Brazile and Ewin, plus transition discipline, to execute that. If Arkansas can keep Hawai‘i from turning the game into a paint-and-glass slog, Hawai‘i may struggle to score efficiently enough to keep up.

In short, Arkansas has the best player in the matchup, the more explosive and efficient offense, far better ball security, and a preferred tempo that directly attacks Hawai‘i’s pressure and mobility concerns. Hawai‘i’s size and rebounding could make stretches competitive, but the reports suggest Arkansas is better equipped to dictate terms. If the game is played in space with pace, Arkansas should have the upper hand, and that is the most likely outcome from the evidence provided.
